when: Audio, voice, music, ambience, feedback or loudness tasks
goal: Make events recognizable, intelligible and comfortable at varied volume settings.
steps: Inventory audio emitters, sound ownership, and existing volume preferences before making new assets. Separate music, ambience, UI cues and spatial gameplay effects by intent.
Create an audio event matrix: source, trigger, priority, audience, variants, max simultaneity and cleanup owner. Use native Sound/SoundGroup behavior and approved assets.
Duck or deprioritize nonessential audio when safety-critical cues or teammate messages are active. Provide mute and reduced-effects preferences where relevant.
Prefer a few original layered cues over dozens of repeated generic stock sounds; vary sample or pitch mildly without changing the meaning of an alert.
Keep playback client-presentational when possible; only server-confirmed game state may trigger rewarding or consequential sounds.
proof: Solo and two-client audible event ordering, mute/reset and repeated-shift cleanup.
Document source/license of every imported sound and measure actual playback behavior rather than asserting quality from file presence.
anti: Do not let music drown spoken/gameplay information or make an audio cue grant rewards.

when: Camera movement, framing, obstruction, motion sickness or respawn issues
goal: Keep important action readable while respecting default Roblox camera controls.
steps: State the viewing contract: first or third person, action framing, allowed zoom, lock-on if any, and mobile/controller parity.
Use the Roblox camera module/default camera when it already satisfies the contract; add owned offsets rather than replacing the whole system.
Calculate damping from delta time, maintain clamped motion, and solve obstruction without piercing walls or losing aim.
Keep cosmetic shake and recoil independent from authoritative movement; make additive contributions reversible and coexist with other camera systems.
Provide reduced motion and avoid per-frame event connection churn.
proof: Repeated jump/landing and respawn test verifies camera returns to baseline without drift.
Observe desktop/controller/touch rotation and enclosed spaces at low and high frame rates.
anti: Never write camera offsets without an explicit restore path or treat render events as a source of gameplay truth.

when: Any concept art, meshes, textures, sound assets, props or character appearance
goal: Convert a coherent art direction into reusable, provenanced in-game assets.
steps: Inventory existing assets and establish an art bible: silhouettes, materials, palette, camera, target devices and genre-specific visual priorities.
Choose a representative hero asset and review it in-game before scaling production. Concept images are references, not geometry or proof of integration.
Maintain an asset ledger including author, origin/license, editable source, export, target Roblox template, dimensions and expected draw cost.
Prefer Blender for meaningful custom 3D modeling; prefer Roblox primitives and native UI for simpler structures. Normalize pivots, attachments and units.
Create asset families with intentional modular reuse, then integrate through the chosen authoritative source pipeline.
proof: Validate exports, material mapping, alignment, lighting, silhouette legibility and import ownership in actual Roblox Studio.
Produce a contact sheet or viewport evidence plus the manifest for every completed asset family.
anti: Never copy unlicensed Toolbox/script content or equate a nice render with a functional game asset.

when: Actions mechanically work but feel unresponsive or unsatisfying
goal: Give important actions timely feedback without changing server decisions.
steps: Identify meaningful player actions and rank their importance: input acknowledgment, task progress, success, failure and danger.
For each action choose at most a few matching feedback channels: sound, animation, light, UI, haptics, particles or a very small camera response.
Attach feedback to a known authoritative result for rewards, combat outcomes and work completion; speculative client previews must remain cosmetic.
Tune response timing and intensity on the lowest intended device tier. Add reduced-motion and low-effects options.
Compare adjacent actions and remove feedback that masks danger, reduces readability or becomes tiring after a full session.
proof: Record input-to-feedback behavior, repeated-action spam behavior and independent reduced-effects verification.
Test actual controller, touch and multiplayer observer views when available.
anti: Do not freeze a shared simulation to sell a local impact or stack uncontrolled camera shake.

when: Screen hierarchy, onboarding, menu flow or accessibility decisions
goal: Make the next action obvious and every important screen navigable.
steps: Map the first-session path from join through first success and next-round choice; define the job of each screen and remove duplicate decisions.
Build one coherent typographic and spatial system: information priority, contrast, state change, contextual controls and safe margins.
Design without relying on mouse hover or fixed desktop pixels. Plan gamepad focus, touch targets, text scaling and keyboard dismissal.
Use notifications sparingly: critical events interrupt, routine results queue, and player actions receive feedback where attention already is.
For new players introduce one essential mechanic at a time; leave advanced details accessible without blocking play.
proof: Complete a no-instructions first-session walkthrough with the intended devices.
Capture viewport evidence at phone portrait/landscape if supported, tablet, desktop and controller.
anti: Never require precision clicking to complete gameplay or hide essential state inside decorative widgets.

when: Keyboard, mouse, touch, controller, keybinding or action-state tasks
goal: Maintain a single accessible action contract across inputs.
steps: List game verbs before keys: move, interact, jump, sprint, open menu, use ability; separate press, hold, toggle and analog intent.
Prefer Roblox-native character controls and ContextActionService. Preserve platform-reserved controls and existing text-chat focus.
Route intents into validated server actions only when gameplay authority is needed; leave visual-only actions local.
Handle device switching, input cancellation, death, tool ownership, menus, focus loss and respawn as explicit state transitions.
Map mobile controls around thumb regions and test controller focus; avoid duplicate bindings that fire on one press.
proof: Action table plus real input test evidence for keyboard/mouse, gamepad and touch simulation.
Verify input while chat is focused, after a repair is canceled, and after a device switch.
anti: Never equate a synthetic remote call with a real button-press or assume keyboard-only controls suffice.

when: Maps, missions, traversal, encounters, pacing or exploration layout
goal: Make objectives traversable, readable, varied and appropriately paced.
steps: Start with player movement dimensions, camera clearance and abilities. Translate those metrics into route widths, gaps and vertical access.
Block out the full critical path using simple geometry before visual detail. Add safe alternates when a moving door/elevator may fail.
Design a tension curve with breathing room, learning beats and a deliberate finale; avoid continuously maxed-out challenge.
Measure travel times to objectives, spawn-to-first-action and recovery routes rather than judging layout from overhead art.
Add landmarks, signage and environmental storytelling only after route accessibility and incident ownership are tested.
proof: Trace every required mission path in solo and multiplayer, including obstruction and respawn.
Record travel distances/times from authoritative navigation points for tuning.
anti: Never decorate over interaction envelopes or make required paths rely on random geometry that can soft-lock progress.

when: Slow frames, memory growth, network spikes or heavy asset scenes
goal: Ship measurable improvements against explicit target hardware budgets.
steps: Define target hardware tiers, scene, client count and frame/memory/network goals before optimizing.
Capture a baseline with Roblox MicroProfiler, Script Performance, network stats and memory tools where available.
Locate the dominant cost: scripts, physics, geometry/materials, UI, replication or asset loads. Fix that cost first.
Use pooling, event-driven updates, streaming, LOD and geometry reuse only when a measurement supports them.
Rerun the exact scenario after changes, preserve visual/play quality, and reject changes without convincing improvement.
proof: Report before/after measurements, test platform, session duration and confidence limitations.
Observe long-session join/leave/respawn and real-client frame behavior if accessible.
anti: Do not claim mobile optimization based on a powerful desktop Studio viewport.

when: Unstable objects, collision jitter, tunneling, mass or moving-platform tuning
goal: Make physical behavior consistent and bounded under network conditions.
steps: Choose whether the mechanic truly needs physics or should be scripted/anchored. Specify desired failure modes and interaction limits.
Declare collision groups and query policy separately. Preserve predictable assemblies, attachments and constraints.
Use server authority for consequential physics outcomes; understand when ownership and latency affect observed motion.
Measure velocities, body scale, contact stability and solver behavior under expected load before introducing new forces.
Tune one parameter at a time and ensure cleanup for temporary assemblies and constraints.
proof: Solo/two-client collision observation and representative low/high velocity cases.
Check jitter after pause, respawn, teleport and ownership transfer.
anti: Never use an old physics body mover or Touched-only hit logic without justified constraints and validation.

when: Random maps, spawns, encounters, loot or rotating content
goal: Make procedural content reproducible, fair and verifiable.
steps: Specify the seed source and ownership: match/server, player-specific, or common daily/weekly; never trust a client-chosen authoritative seed.
Generate pure data from a seeded RNG before instantiating geometry, then validate safety rules and budgets.
Check reachability, spawn clearance, loot distributions, enemy capacity and player-count adaptations.
Separate cosmetic variety from consequential randomness; use server-adjudicated outcomes and documented weighting.
Save the seed/parameters for reproducing difficult bug reports and retain deterministic fixture seeds.
proof: Replay identical seeds with matching content and alternate seeds without invalid geometry.
Automate distribution and reachability checks across many representative seeds.
anti: Never let unbounded random retries or global RNG create irreproducible soft-locks.

when: Avatars, rigs, animations, emotes, accessories, respawn and tools
goal: Make characters predictable across spawn cycles, supported rigs and clients.
steps: Define R6/R15 or custom-rig support explicitly and inspect current Humanoid/Animator, default Animate and avatar settings.
Separate player-scoped settings from character-scoped references; cancel pending operations on CharacterRemoving and check generation tokens after yielding.
Use attachments/accessory fitting and compatible Animator tracks; make ownership priority explicit among movement, tools, repairs and emotes.
Prepare graceful fallback for unsupported rig/asset IDs, imperfect hair clearance and missing accessories.
Keep cosmetic animation client-side when safe; never let a visual pose decide authoritative gameplay outcomes.
proof: Spawn, rapid respawn, death, tool swap, outfit change and peer-observer animation matrix.
Verify in-game front/side/back silhouettes and accessory collision/clipping across representative avatars.
anti: Never capture a Humanoid once and assume it remains valid after respawn.

when: Saving player progression, inventory, unlocks, economy or settings
goal: Protect owned player data across failures, retries and cross-server sessions.
steps: Define versioned server-owned schema, bounded values, migration rules and data that must never be client-trusted.
Use UpdateAsync transactions for mutation, appropriate session ownership/leasing, idempotent receipt identifiers and bounded retries.
Separate Studio test stores or test backends from production. Never accidentally modify live player data during QA.
Define on-join, delayed load, autosave, disconnect and shutdown behavior, including outage and owner-loss states.
Publish confirmed save status to UI without fabricating successful writes or discarding valid existing progress.
proof: Migration, duplicate purchase, reconnect, cross-server, rapid leave and injected DataStore failure tests.
Persisted totals must match transaction receipts after simulated retries and server restart.
anti: Never overwrite valid production data with empty defaults because a read failed.

when: Adding or changing Roblox Luau scripts, modules and services
goal: Keep a maintainable server/client/shared structure with testable contracts.
steps: Identify execution location and authoritative owner before writing code. Inspect neighboring modules, remote definitions and conventions.
Use typed Luau where it improves safety and meaningful module boundaries without introducing needless wrappers.
Prefer events and bounded tasks over uncontrolled loops; disconnect signals and destroy temporary instances on lifecycle transitions.
Validate every client-to-server request and avoid trusting replicated attributes written or proposed by clients.
Write or adapt focused tests around state transitions and integrate via the existing Rojo/Studio source path.
proof: StyLua/lint/type checks if available, Rojo build, Studio Output and representative Server & Clients tests.
Report exact changed modules and replayable test cases.
anti: Never place a client-authoritative inventory, damage or currency operation in LocalScripts.

when: Remotes, replication, multiplayer consistency, streaming or anti-exploit review
goal: Make all consequential decisions server-owned and safe under unreliable input.
steps: Inventory every RemoteEvent/RemoteFunction and its caller; write an input and output contract with allowed types and maximum sizes.
For requests validate membership, phase, state, distance, ownership, cooldowns, monotonically increasing identifiers and target existence.
Keep arbitrary client Instances, positions, prices, damage and rewards out of authoritative trust paths; resolve targets server-side.
Minimize broadcast scope and frequency. Account for streaming, out-of-order messages, temporary disconnection and round resets.
Use idempotent and fenced operations when concurrent actions or economic writes can race.
proof: Test expected and malicious requests, rate-limit abuse, simultaneous players, joining mid-round and disconnects.
Validate cross-client agreement by reading server-owned state, not by trusting locally displayed UI.
anti: Never treat server-side type checks alone as authorization or let client-provided results settle wins and rewards.

when: Assemblies, raycasts, overlap queries, collision flags, network ownership
goal: Make geometric interactions safe, precise and affordable.
steps: Choose raycast, overlap, constraints or contact events according to required accuracy and trust, not convenience.
Create a clear collision matrix; distinguish CanCollide, CanTouch and CanQuery for every important part.
Filter raycasts/overlap targets to valid gameplay objects and check distances and line of sight on the server where needed.
Keep cosmetic meshes noncollidable when dedicated bounds/collision proxies provide the actual gameplay geometry.
Bound query frequency and instance lifetimes, and test moving assemblies at expected speeds.
proof: Server/client geometry agreement and no unexpected collisions in critical routes.
Confirm physics ownership, constraints and reset cleanup in multi-client Studio.
anti: Never use Workspace visual prop placement as an authoritative gameplay hitbox by accident.

when: Editing live Studio places, Rojo mapping, imported assets or publishing private QA
goal: Keep one source of truth and distinguish actual runtime evidence from offline success.
steps: Before modifying a place identify active DataModel, universe/place identity, audience and authoritative source (Rojo versus Studio).
Keep production code and templates in source control; treat disposable Studio fixtures and temporary Workspace assets as transient.
Use native Studio for hierarchy, import, input simulation, runtime Output and Server & Clients validation. Map tools to correct execution contexts.
Preserve a one-editor/one-Studio-operator lock during automated work; reconcile saved source after native editor actions.
Before any private publication compare all production scripts/assets to intended source, save a recovery copy and record actual published version.
proof: Pass a verification ladder: static/build, solo, multi-client, cross-device emulation, actual device if available, private cloud save.
Record which environment produced each result and never promote waived tests into passes.
anti: Never publish publicly based on private QA evidence or confuse a saved local place with a published experience.

when: Creating ScreenGuis, menus, HUD, settings, tooltips, shops or chat-related UI
goal: Make all user-facing interface states editable, usable and resilient.
steps: Inspect existing StarterGui/PlayerGui templates and UI ownership; avoid rebuilding every screen with monolithic scripts.
Use scalable UDim2 layouts, constraints, safe-area-aware insets and design tokens; account for longer labels and localization.
Keep UI state a presentation of server-confirmed facts where needed, and use Activated plus explicit gamepad focus handling.
Keep screen transitions reversible, distinguish loading/failed/confirmed operations and release event connections on teardown.
Treat TextChatService and Roblox core UI restrictions as platform responsibilities; style without bypassing filtering or privacy.
proof: Keyboard, phone, gamepad focus, screen resize, respawn and multiple-open cycles.
Check clipping, contrast, readable text, touch target sizes and emergency message priority.
anti: Never bind purchase success to a local button click or assume UI success means a server operation persisted.

when: Choosing specialist playbooks for a new task or project phase
goal: Load only the guidance needed rather than every reference at once.
steps: Classify work by task risk (design, implementation, bug, security, art, release) and Roblox subsystem before selecting references.
Pick one primary discipline playbook plus at most two supporting ones; add security and verification for state-changing paths.
Reuse selection for adjacent tasks; reclassify only when the work genuinely pivots.
If a specialist reference or connector is unavailable, use the existing engine workflow and state the limitation rather than hunting indefinitely.
Never allow a generic framework recipe to override the project-specific AGENTS.md or current official Roblox API behavior.
proof: Explain selected playbooks in one concise routing note when it materially changes the plan.
Confirm no conflicting source ownership or duplicate tool installation was introduced.
anti: Do not load the entire playbook library into context or start from a skill search on every minor edit.

when: Schema evolution, backups, restore, settings or checkpoint persistence
goal: Make saved state small, versioned, migratable and recoverable.
steps: Separate transient session state from durable server-owned state and identify data-loss impact of every change.
Define schema version, default policy, validation and pure migration functions before adding new fields.
Use idempotent writes and version-aware conflict handling; for Roblox online progression, defer to Roblox DataStore semantics rather than filesystem rename patterns.
Create backup/restore and rollback plans for incompatible changes. Avoid storing Instance references as profile data.
Use load failure and stale-data states in UI rather than silently resetting a profile.
proof: Test fresh, old schema, malformed, missing, partial-failure and rollback scenarios.
Verify cross-server re-entry and saved inventory invariants under duplicate operations.
anti: Never confuse local file durability with Roblox cloud persistence or assume a DataStore outage is a new-user profile.

when: Choosing implementations, dependencies, complexity and refactors
goal: Find the smallest end-to-end correct solution, not the smallest patch.
steps: Before coding, trace the requested behavior across actual caller, server, client, tests, assets, UI, profile migrations and Studio deployment.
Compare reuse of an existing module or Roblox API against new code; choose the least complex approach that completes the contract.
Intensity levels are review depth, not permission to omit work: light for tiny UI text, standard for ordinary systems, intensive for risky multiplayer, persistence, migrations and release.
Make a bounded diff, then inspect broken callers and orphaned assets. Remove speculative abstractions and one-off libraries.
If a simplification reduces security, validation, accessibility, maintainability or data recoverability, reject it.
proof: Diff reviewed for necessary changes, test evidence and rollback risk.
Rationale for any new dependency, service or abstraction.
anti: Do not mistake fewer lines or fewer tests for better engineering.

when: Reviewing a patch, PR, feature or recent commit
goal: Catch errors and unnecessary complexity before integration.
steps: Identify the starting revision and proposed diff; read the full affected call chain and external contracts.
Check correctness, remote trust boundaries, concurrency, player profiles, initialization and teardown under expected load.
Look for unnecessary wrappers, duplicated state, new dependencies and abandoned flags, then propose removal only if safe.
Assign each finding a severity, file location, reproduction or proof, and minimally sufficient correction.
Review tests independently of the implementer and rerun cases after high-risk fixes.
proof: Actionable findings with grounded paths and priority; a clean report states exactly what was checked.
Security, persistence and multi-client risks verified independently.
anti: Do not write a style-only critique while ignoring exploitable or data-loss bugs.

when: Auditing a full Roblox project or inherited repository
goal: Identify product, architectural and production risks in ranked order.
steps: Start with README, AGENTS, Rojo mapping, build tools, critical gameplay flows, profiles, remotes, CI and private publication trail.
Map modules and their ownership to reveal duplicated managers, circular requires, dead assets and unbounded services.
Sample high-consequence code deeply: authoritative combat/rewards, client remotes, data stores, loops, memory and asset provenance.
Distinguish confirmed defects from concerns requiring Studio reproduction. Avoid a superficial list of everything that could happen.
Give a ranked repair backlog with a concise deletion/merge suggestion only where behavior can be preserved.
proof: Audit scope, commit inspected, missing evidence and priority-ranked findings.
A regression plan for any recommended deletion or major consolidation.
anti: Never rewrite an entire game merely because its original organization differs from your preferred architecture.

when: Collecting deliberate shortcuts, waivers and post-release debt
goal: Make compromises visible, time-bounded and actionable.
steps: Search TODO, FIXME, waiver records, deferred animation slots, compatibility fallbacks and release blockers.
For each entry record source file, reason, user impact, current risk, date, owner and objective exit criteria.
Separate acceptable aesthetic polish debt from security, player-data and public-release blockers.
Link each debt item to a tested project milestone; remove entries only after evidence of resolution.
Keep the list short and factual so it guides releases rather than becoming a duplicate roadmap.
proof: Debt count by severity plus exact references and next action.
No silent closure of waived or untested items.
anti: Never use a TODO comment to excuse a known critical release blocker.

when: Assessing refactor or optimization gains
goal: Measure the effect of lean decisions instead of claiming imaginary savings.
steps: Choose comparable metrics before change: file/module count, affected calls, test time, load latency, CPU, memory or frame stability.
Compare equal builds and scenes with consistent avatar/device/client counts.
Account for code removed and new maintenance burden while retaining validation and user-facing quality.
Record test environment and uncertainty; if metrics cannot be collected, state that they are unknown.
Do not perform optimization work solely to improve the scoreboard.
proof: Table of baseline, follow-up, delta, method and any unmeasured variables.
Reproduction commands when measurements were automatic.
anti: Never fabricate performance percentages or imply an external benchmark applies to this project.

when: Selecting development review depth or explaining the system
goal: Choose the appropriate diligence without changing user permissions.
steps: Light mode: contained copy/style edit with no persistence, networking or new authorization paths.
Standard mode: most implementation tasks; audit caller impact, tests, recoverability and UI parity.
Intensive mode: economy, anti-exploit, networking, schema migration, cross-device controls, public launch and major architecture.
Every mode retains correctness, security, testing, accessibility and data safety. Intensive adds independent review and broader scenarios.
Choose modes from task risk, not how many tokens are left.
proof: Record risk level and why in the task plan; downgrade only after proven lower risk.
anti: Modes must never silently change hooks, marketplace permissions or publish access.

when: Writing final status, evidence or handoff summaries
goal: Tell an owner what changed, what passed, what remains and what to do next.
steps: Start with actual status: complete, partial, blocked or not started, never a ceremonial claim.
Identify changed work, source revision, runtime/publication identity and the smallest relevant test results.
Preserve exact commands, filenames, flags, error text and negations even in short summaries.
Separate observed facts from plans and unverified assumptions. Give one concrete next action when necessary.
For irreversible actions, permissions and security concerns favor full sentences and explicit cautions.
proof: An unfamiliar developer can resume using the report without re-interviewing the implementer.
anti: Never shorten technical payloads or let compactness hide missing verification.

when: Unclear or ambitious game ideas, new creative direction or major feature choices
goal: Reach an approved, testable game identity before autonomous building.
steps: Inspect any existing project and the user's specific inspirations before proposing unrelated concepts.
Ask focused questions in a conversation rather than a massive form; separate goals, audience, genre, replay loop, camera, platforms, budget and taste.
Present 2–3 coherent alternatives and evaluate scope, originality, player promise, competitive identity and Roblox policy risks.
Summarize final decisions, rejected ideas and unresolved choices into an owner-readable creative brief and acceptance tests.
Ask for approval of the complete directive once; allow safe implementation autonomy after approval within its boundaries.
proof: Approved concept brief with loop, one polished vertical slice, constraints and no unapproved speculative mechanics.
Clear examples of what the game is and is not.
anti: Do not start coding based on a vague mood board or pretend that auto-generated art establishes gameplay feasibility.

when: Parallel investigations, assets or testing with non-overlapping ownership
goal: Get genuine independent progress without clobbering shared files.
steps: Decompose the work into tasks with separate files, outputs and contracts; identify serial dependencies before dispatch.
Give each agent exact scope, baseline revision, acceptance, evidence format and prohibited changes.
Allow parallel analysis broadly; allow parallel edits only with isolated worktrees or explicit file ownership.
Centralize source integration and run a fresh combined test after all agent results arrive.
If subagents are unavailable, execute the same ownership plan sequentially instead of claiming parallel work.
proof: Owner/agent matrix showing outputs, changed paths, conflicts, tests and integration commit.
Combined regression results beyond individual agent success claims.
anti: Do not assign two editors to the same Roblox Studio place or module concurrently.

when: Implementing an accepted multi-step task plan
goal: Complete scoped increments with checkpoints instead of endless planning.
steps: Confirm the approved design, current HEAD, clean or preserved worktree, environment and required dependencies.
For each task: reproduce expected behavior, create a failing test if practical, implement bounded changes, run tests and record proof.
Mark progress only after tests, diff review and source integration; keep next-step context in a durable ledger.
Select any optional tools once, then focus on implementation. Replan if evidence contradicts the spec rather than forcing broken work.
At a deadline, checkpoint partial changes safely, preserve exact resume instructions and stop further edits.
proof: Progress ledger with complete/partial/blocked state, commit identities and commands.
The latest working checkpoint can be restored without reconstructing conversation history.
anti: Never mark a task done because code was written, an agent said done or a local mock passed.

when: Committing, pushing, merging, creating PRs or finalizing a development branch
goal: Preserve history and hand off a verified, reviewable change set.
steps: Inspect git status, diff and branch tracking; run the required tests before staging.
Confirm destination branch and user authorization for push/PR; never infer permission to force-push or publish a Roblox place.
Create a focused commit with a meaningful summary and evidence reference; push only after verifying no secrets or generated junk.
Report commit SHA, branch, remote, push status and any known conflict. Do not erase uncommitted other-author work.
Keep Roblox place publication, Git push and production launch as three separate operations with separate proof.
proof: Exact commit SHA, push output and recovery instructions.
Post-integration regression results when merging or rebasing.
anti: Never call an unpublished place deployed, or treat a GitHub push as a Roblox production release.

when: Handling peer, user or automated code-review suggestions
goal: Use reviewer feedback as evidence, not unquestionable authority.
steps: Read the entire report, locate the actual code path and reproduce any claimed defect where possible.
Classify correctness, safety, performance, architecture and preference suggestions separately.
Accept valid changes, challenge unsupported refactors with measurements, and ask only for genuinely ambiguous owner choices.
Implement accepted findings one at a time with tests; make exceptions explicit and track rejected points.
Keep the reply factual and avoid performative agreement.
proof: Traceable disposition for each issue: fixed, rejected with reason, deferred with owner decision, or blocked.
New verification after each high-risk correction.
anti: Never add a new dependency or rewrite working code solely because a generic reviewer preferred it.

when: Before significant commits, merges or game release milestones
goal: Find defects that the implementer may have normalized.
steps: Give reviewers requirements, base/head revisions, changed files, verified cases and the areas where confidence is low.
Use at least one reviewer focused on exploits, persistent data and concurrency for consequential multiplayer changes.
Ask for file-and-line-grounded findings with severity, reproduction or reasoning and test recommendations.
Reconcile feedback against the actual source; fix critical/high issues and rerun tests.
For a release review, examine end-to-end first-session play and studio/publication parity, not just code style.
proof: Independent review summary, issue dispositions and final pass/fail gate.
Explicit statement of coverage limits and reviewer independence.
anti: Do not use an agent thumbs-up as proof that actual multiplayer or mobile tests ran.

when: Delegating independent implementation tasks to Codex agents
goal: Preserve fresh focus, source ownership and verifiable integration.
steps: Split approved design into small deliverables with stable interfaces, filenames, test commands, and a clear handoff shape.
Assign one implementer and a distinct reviewer to high-risk tasks; worktrees or explicit no-overlap rules prevent collisions.
Require each implementer to return changed paths, tests run, unresolved failures and actual evidence.
Integrate only completed revisions, perform a fresh combined test, record task state and release file ownership.
Use sequential execution when tools cannot provide independent agents or isolation.
proof: Progress ledger and supervisor acceptance linked to exact commits and test reports.
No duplicate writes and no undisclosed bypass of project permissions.
anti: Never let subagent prompts grant privileges beyond the owner's approved scope.

when: Bug, flake, crash, failing test, broken Studio behavior or regression
goal: Understand the failure before changing the code.
steps: Reproduce the issue and record exact inputs, client count, game state, device, error and revision.
Trace data and control flow from symptom to source across server/client boundary; compare a known-good checkpoint if available.
Write one falsifiable hypothesis and minimal probe; observe whether it explains the failure.
Fix the responsible cause with the smallest complete change, including affected callers and cleanup.
Rerun the reproduction and a neighboring regression test; remove probes and temporary fixtures.
proof: Before/after reproduction, root-cause explanation, diff and verification environment.
Known remaining uncertainty clearly stated.
anti: Do not apply a third speculative patch without investigating why earlier hypotheses failed.

when: Feature logic, behavior changes, bug fixes or contract refactors
goal: Define behavior in executable checks before trusting implementation.
steps: State the user-visible behavior and server invariants; choose a small automated or isolated Studio fixture suited to the risk.
Create an initial check that fails for the intended reason or capture an existing failing reproduction.
Implement the minimum change, rerun the failing test, then run nearby regression cases.
Refactor duplication only after the behavior passes and remains understandable.
Where Studio-only visual behavior cannot be unit tested, define explicit manual/automated viewport acceptance before editing.
proof: Failing baseline and passing follow-up with actual run output, plus runtime verification where required.
No false report of a failing test when the test never executed.
anti: Tests that assert internal implementation details cannot substitute for gameplay or networking correctness.

when: Parallel tasks, experiments, risky refactors or branch isolation
goal: Keep experiments recoverable without corrupting the main working tree.
steps: Inspect existing Git worktrees, uncommitted changes and repository policy before creating another workspace.
Prefer the active approved worktree; create a new one only when isolation adds value and a safe directory is available.
Use separate checkout/branch per isolated editor and share results through commits/patches, not simultaneous writes.
Run a clean baseline build and test in the new worktree before edits.
Keep worktrees until changes are integrated and recoverability is confirmed; clean up only with deliberate authorization.
proof: Workspace path, branch, base SHA, baseline checks, final integration SHA.
No data loss of existing working tree or Studio saved file.
anti: Never run broad destructive Git clean/reset commands merely to prepare a workspace.

when: Starting a new task and deciding what process guidance to use
goal: Route based on task and risk without inflating context.
steps: Read the master skill once and identify the current stage: meeting, design lock, implementation, debugging, art, review or release.
Load only relevant original practice references using the routing map; a new task domain may add one or two more.
Apply instructions in order: owner permissions and current repo rules, approved design, engine requirements, selected playbooks.
If an optional external skill or connector is absent, use this package and native tooling rather than repeated setup attempts.
Do not silently change skill settings, global Codex hooks or unrelated project configuration.
proof: Selection remains stable across adjacent subtasks and can be explained in one sentence when asked.
anti: Never replace game-specific approvals with a broad instruction such as full autonomy.

when: Before saying done, fixed, tested, deployed or ready
goal: Make claims no stronger than fresh evidence.
steps: For each completion claim specify the test or artifact that could verify it and the exact expected result.
Run the test in the relevant environment; read the full result and check failures instead of relying on truncated output.
Distinguish static syntax, Rojo build, Studio simulation, multi-client runtime, physical device and published private cloud evidence.
When an unavailable API or human/device check blocks verification, label it unverified and leave the corresponding gate open.
Before a release claim cross-check latest Git source SHA against actual saved/published Studio scripts and asset templates.
proof: Verification matrix with test, date, revision, environment, result and evidence path.
No known blocking issues hidden behind a cumulative pass count.
anti: Never turn user-waived tests into passes or interpret absence of errors as proof of playability.

when: Converting an approved game design into executable work
goal: Build the smallest polished end-to-end vertical slice before scale.
steps: Decompose the spec into gameplay core, network security, playable world, player feedback, progression, art, device QA and release gates.
For every task define dependencies, exact source ownership, measurable acceptance, test method, failure recovery and exit artifact.
Prioritize a complete playable loop with progression and repeated sessions before decorative breadth.
Group tasks so one programmer or agent can finish and verify without touching many unrelated systems.
Record rejected nice-to-have features and owner decision gates to prevent scope creep during autonomous execution.
proof: Plan with task IDs, priorities, dependency graph, evidence slots and stop/resume checkpoints.
Each task ends at a reproducible verification checkpoint.
anti: Do not measure plan completeness by number of features or confuse planning with doing.

when: Designing, modifying, packaging or validating the reusable skill system
goal: Keep each instruction module discoverable, testable and maintainable.
steps: Identify the exact failure the new playbook should prevent, then capture a baseline scenario where generic advice is insufficient.
Write narrow trigger wording, practical steps, evidence expectations and anti-patterns in original language.
Test on unrelated Roblox genres and failure conditions; compare behavior with and without the new guidance where tools permit.
Check no duplicate names, circular routing, broken relative links, licensing/credit errors or excessive default context.
Separate quick guidance from deep references and scripts; do not require users to install irrelevant dependencies.
proof: Pressure-scenario test results, static packaging validation and documented limitations.
Manifest coverage updated for any new or retired playbook.
anti: Do not publish an untested skill as a guaranteed autonomous game builder.

source: Impeccable referenced in Upkeep AGENTS.md; source not accessible
when: Final visual review or stylization consistency tasks
goal: Make a coherent world feel authored rather than randomly assembled.
steps: Select a small reference frame representing the game tone, values, shape language, palette and character-to-world scale.
Compare playable camera views across menu, first five minutes, representative action and results; inspect clutter, hierarchy and silhouette.
Correct visual inconsistencies in prioritized order: blocking/readability, asset proportions, material coherence, animation, lighting, then micro-polish.
Compare improvements to mobile-sized views and the actual in-game render instead of approving only large concept images.
Keep the art style original and avoid recreating competing Roblox experiences.
proof: Before/after images or Studio observations with device viewport and actual asset source identity.
No text clipping, critical icon confusion or decorative occlusion in core routes.
anti: Do not interpret generic visual design advice as permission to import unlicensed assets.
